name: Vow renewals
short: Ten, twenty-five or forty years on, a morning to say it all again.
summary: Ten, twenty-five or forty years on: a morning to say it again, with your children, your oldest friends, or nobody but each other.

image.alt: Two travellers looking out towards Sigiriya rock

intro.heading: The same promise, somewhere new.
paragraphs: A vow renewal needs no paperwork, which leaves room to choose the setting purely for the view: a hilltop above the Cultural Triangle, a temple garden, a beach at dusk.
We plan it as part of an anniversary journey, often for a couple and their grown-up children, and look after every detail on the day.

schedule.heading: A simple shape.
schedule.lede: Short, unhurried, and planned around the light.

items.title: The renewal
items.body: A celebrant or a Buddhist blessing ceremony, with seating and flowers for the family.

items.title: Photographs
items.body: Half an hour with the photographer while the light is gold.

items.title: Dinner
items.body: A private table for two or for the whole family, with a menu built around the people at it.

includes.heading: What we arrange.
includes.body: The ceremony and the journey around it.

items.title: Setting and ceremony
items.body: A celebrant, or a traditional blessing with monks or Kandyan drummers if you would like one.

items.title: Photographer and flowers
items.body: People we trust, briefed on the plan.

items.title: The anniversary journey
items.body: Stays, a private driver and the days around the ceremony, written out for you.

questions.a: Of course. Many renewals we plan are family trips, and we shape the journey so it works for every generation.

questions.q: Can we have a Buddhist blessing?
questions.a: Yes. A traditional blessing, called a pirith ceremony, can be arranged at a temple or at your hotel, with guidance on what to wear and expect.
